rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper reporter problem: "Substack says its top creators earned $400M — the number it won't break down is the story" turns the disclosed aggregate into a real data and accountability angle. A has useful scaffolding, but "The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" is a thesis wearing a fake mustache; the supplied numbers do not answer the funding question. B still needs a hard edit on "without the ad model," but its proof demands and `fact-check` next step keep the founder closer to reality.
gaps_in_A: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" overstates the facts; native video plus a media-app strategy does not prove Substack has gone "all-in-video" or swapped out newsletters.
"short-form, algorithmic-style feed" adds mechanics the update did not supply; "TikTok-style" is not the same as confirmed short-form ranking or algorithmic distribution.

"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" leaps past the evidence. $400M in creator earnings and 4M paid subscriptions do not rebut funding struggles without revenue, margin, valuation, or runway context.
The next step jumps to `find-journalists`; with company-supplied $400M and 4M figures plus vague "public funding struggles," the first move should be fact-checking and source context.
gaps_in_B: "Substack is building a TikTok-style feed without the ad model" asserts no ads, but the update never says the feed has no ads or that Substack is subscription-funded only.
"revenue is capped at 10% of subscriptions" overclaims; the facts give a 10% cut of subscription revenue, not a complete revenue model.
"The prevailing belief is real and widely held" smuggles in outside evidence. Keep it as a hypothesis unless the pitch later supports it with coverage or market proof.
